findings.location: design.md#Decision: Birth dates live on the profile
findings.recommendation: Tie retention to the purpose, not to the profile (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e), storage limitation): add a requirement and a scenario for opting out — when a member turns birthday greetings off, `birthday` and `phone` are cleared from `profiles` — and a task that implements and tests it. Today a member who withdraws keeps both fields stored for the life of the account, with no use left for them; the spec only covers "the phone number was removed", not withdrawal of the opt-in.
findings.title: Birthday and phone are kept after the member opts out

findings.location: design.md#Decision: Birth dates live on the profile
findings.recommendation: State how long the nightly backups holding `birthday` and `phone` are kept and how an erased or withdrawn member's values leave them (backup expiry period, or re-application of erasures on restore). As written, a member's birthday and phone number cleared from `profiles` survive in every backup with no defined end (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e), Art. 17).
findings.title: No retention or erasure rule for the copies in nightly backups

findings.location: design.md#Decision: Greetings are sent by SMS through Textly
findings.recommendation: Send Textly only the phone number and the message text it must deliver (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), data minimisation). Nothing in the spec says the greeting carries the member's name; if it must, say so in the requirement and send the name only inside the message body. Otherwise every opted-in member's display name goes to a third-party processor for no stated purpose.
findings.title: Display name sent to Textly though the greeting does not need it

findings.evidence:
A daily job selects the profiles whose birthday is today and posts each
phone number and display name to Textly's API (hosted in the United
States), which sends the message.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Greetings are sent by SMS through Textly
findings.recommendation: Question for the team: Textly is a new processor outside the EEA. Record the processing agreement (GDPR Art. 28) and the transfer mechanism (Chapter V — adequacy decision such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, or standard contractual clauses) in the design, or pick an EEA-hosted SMS provider. Only the controller can confirm what was decided.
findings.title: Transfer of phone numbers to a US processor has no stated safeguard

findings.evidence: Members enjoy being remembered; marketing wants birthday messages.
findings.recommendation: Question for the team: state the purpose (a member-requested greeting, or marketing) and the lawful basis (presumably consent through the opt-in, GDPR Art. 6(1)(a)) for `birthday` and `phone`. If the messages serve marketing, the SMS needs prior consent under the ePrivacy Directive and the phone number must not be reused for other campaigns; say so in the proposal.
findings.title: Purpose and lawful basis of the new data are not stated
